name: Palladian Construction Loadframe Exo-Rig — 'The Mule'
description:
The Loadframe Exo-Rig is a full-body industrial exoskeleton developed by Palladian Construction for heavy labor in GLMZ's perpetual construction and demolition zones. Worn as a suit, it amplifies the operator's physical output by a factor of twelve through a network of hydraulic actuators and strain-anticipation servos, allowing a single worker to lift, carry, and place loads that would otherwise require heavy machinery. The rig's steel-composite frame distributes weight across a broad base plate system, preventing the ground sinkage common in soft rubble terrain. Palladian designed the Mule for efficiency, not elegance — it is loud, heavy, and visually imposing in a way that reflects its purpose entirely.

The Mule's Strain Anticipation System is its most technically sophisticated feature — a suite of force sensors and a predictive algorithm that reads the operator's movement intent from micro-muscle activations and pre-loads the actuators before the full movement is initiated. This eliminates the half-second lag common in older exo-rigs and gives experienced operators the sensation of the suit moving with them rather than after them. The system was designed for load-bearing tasks but translates effectively to combat applications, where the pre-loaded actuators allow strike speeds and force outputs that exceed what unaugmented humans can track and respond to. Palladian does not advertise this application.

The Mule is everywhere in GLMZ — construction sites, salvage yards, port facilities, and disaster response operations. Because it is classified as industrial equipment rather than a weapon system, licensing requirements are comparatively light, making it accessible at lower tiers than most military-grade hardware. This has led to widespread adoption outside its intended context. Modified Mules appear in underground fighting circuits, in the hands of gang enforcers, and in the toolkit of any outfit that needs someone to walk through a wall.

specifications.power_source: Hot-swap hydraulic battery cells, 10-hour operational life per set
specifications.hardpoints: 4 external modular attachment points (tool, weapon, or cargo rack compatible)
specifications.armor_rating: Industrial grade — resistant to crushing, fragmentation, and thermal contact; not rated for direct ballistic engagement

tactical_use: In sanctioned use, the Mule handles structural material movement, demolition assist, and disaster extrication. In the field, operators use it to breach reinforced doors and interior walls, create cover by repositioning heavy objects, and engage in close-quarters combat where the strength amplification makes the operator effectively unkillable by unaugmented opponents. The hardpoint system accepts weapon mounts, and aftermarket attachment kits are widely available that convert the rig's tool ports to support heavy firearms, breaching tools, or improvised armor plating. A fully modified Mule is a budget alternative to military combat exo-rigs.
cultural_context: The Mule occupies an interesting cultural space — it is simultaneously a symbol of physical labor, of working-class endurance, and of a certain kind of dangerous competence. Construction workers who spend careers in Palladian rigs develop an intimate relationship with the equipment, personalizing their units extensively. The same rigs, stripped and modified, appear in GLMZ's fighting circuits where Mule bouts — two operators in modified rigs — draw significant underground betting interest. Corporate security contractors who encounter a modified Mule in the field report it as one of the more unsettling engagements, because the visual language of the rig says 'construction worker' right up until it doesn't.
story_hooks: A Palladian construction site has gone silent mid-project. The last communication mentioned the crew's Mule rigs behaving strangely — moving on their own during shutdown cycles.
An underground Mule fighting circuit has been accepting bets from corporate accounts, suggesting someone is laundering money through the sport. The fighters themselves don't know.

A modified Mule was used to breach the vault of a GLMZ financial node. The modification is too sophisticated for street-level work — someone with serious engineering resources built this rig specifically for the job.
A construction worker's Mule recorded something it shouldn't have during a demolition contract — the building being torn down wasn't empty, and the rig's sensor logs prove it.
